facts.statement: The research examined how giving piracetam after an injury affects a rat model of mild traumatic brain injury.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Twenty-one male Wistar rats were split into three groups of seven: a control group, a group with mild brain trauma, and a group treated with piracetam.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The piracetam group received a 200 mg/kg dose via injection one hour after the injury.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Researchers measured levels of specific proteins and markers in the hippocampus and blood, and examined tissue samples from the cortex, CA3, and dentate gyrus.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Mild brain trauma worsened anxiety, depression, and memory scores and caused changes in inflammation, oxidation, and cell death markers, but did not change general movement.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Piracetam treatment reduced the negative behavioral and biochemical effects of the injury, bringing most measures closer to those of the control group.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Tissue damage improved only partially and varied by brain area, with the most consistent benefits seen in the CA3 region.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Compared to the injured group, piracetam lowered markers for glial cells and immune cells while raising a marker for synapses.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: There was no significant difference in VEGF levels between the piracetam-treated rats and the injured rats after statistical adjustment.
facts.subject: animals
